meta.title: Phenomenology of remote sensing from space
meta.subtitle: A source × interaction grid of every established technique, the empty cells, and the concepts that could fill them, with technology readiness per entry
meta.caveat: TRL values are my estimates against NASA definitions, judged for use from space in the stated application, from knowledge through mid-2026 and checked against mission status and the literature on 2026-10-17. They remain hypotheses, and the TRL of a technique is not the TRL of any specific instrument. Items marked verify sit where a scheduled data release or launch will move the number. Novelty claims were the weakest field: of thirteen rated high, one survived a search, and each concept's prior-art field now names what was found.

sources.note: Reflected and transmitted sunlight; Fraunhofer lines; the Sun itself as target

sources.name: Earth emission
sources.note: Thermal IR, microwave brightness temperature, airglow and aurora, sub-mm limb emission

sources.name: Own transmitter
sources.note: Radar, lidar, laser ranging, sounders; ground lasers pointed up count here

sources.name: Signals of opportunity
sources.note: GNSS, comm downlinks and crosslinks, broadcast RF, anthropogenic light

sources.name: Natural transients
sources.note: Lightning, gamma-ray flashes, quakes and explosions coupling into the atmosphere

sources.name: Cosmic sources
sources.note: Stars, quasars, pulsars, cosmic rays and the secondaries they induce

sources.name: Fields & particles
sources.note: Gravity, magnetic and electric fields, plasma, energetic particles

interactions.name: Reflection
interactions.note: Photons leave a surface unchanged in wavelength, in a direction set by surface geometry
interactions.physics: Light returns from an interface without a change of wavelength. The specular component follows the Fresnel equations and the surface slope distribution; the diffuse component is described by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF). This grid uses reflection for the geometric-optics regime, where the reflector is much larger than the wavelength, and elastic scattering for particles and volumes whose response depends on the size parameter.
interactions.observable: Spectral radiance as a function of wavelength, view angle and illumination angle; parallax between views.
interactions.yields: Surface composition and condition from spectral reflectance (albedo, vegetation indices, mineral absorption features in the reflected continuum); surface roughness and slicks from the specular component (glint); topography from parallax; change from repeat imaging.
interactions.limit: Needs an illuminator, so the Sun sets the diurnal and seasonal sampling. Atmospheric scattering and absorption must be removed to reach surface reflectance. No information from beneath the first scattering surface. Sensor-sun-target geometry changes the answer, which is why BRDF is a correction for some techniques and the observable for others.

interactions.name: Absorption
interactions.note: Photons removed from a beam at wavelengths matching a transition in the medium
interactions.physics: A gas, liquid or solid removes photons at wavelengths matching electronic, vibrational or rotational transitions. Transmission follows Beer–Lambert, T = exp(−τ), with optical depth τ the product of absorber amount and cross-section. Line width carries pressure (Lorentz broadening) and temperature (Doppler broadening); line ratios carry temperature.
interactions.observable: Depth and shape of absorption lines or bands against a known continuum: the solar spectrum, a laser line, thermal emission from below, a star, or lightning.
interactions.yields: Column amounts from line depth; vertical distribution from line shape or from a set of channels with different weighting functions; temperature from line ratios. The O2 A-band at 760 nm serves as an airmass and cloud-height reference because its abundance is known.
interactions.limit: Requires a known background continuum. Spectral resolution must resolve the line relative to its width, which drives instrument size. Strong lines saturate. In cloud and aerosol the photon path length is ambiguous, which converts a scattering problem into an absorption error.

interactions.name: Emission
interactions.note: The target radiates on its own: thermal, chemiluminescent, electronic, or anthropogenic
interactions.physics: No illuminator is needed. Thermal emission follows the Planck function scaled by emissivity, and in the Rayleigh–Jeans regime (microwave) brightness temperature is linear in physical temperature. Airglow is chemiluminescence from recombination at 85–300 km; aurora is collisional excitation by precipitating particles; lightning is a hot plasma channel; terrestrial gamma-ray flashes are bremsstrahlung; nighttime lights and RF emitters are anthropogenic sources treated here as signals of opportunity.
interactions.observable: Spectral radiance or brightness temperature versus wavelength, view angle and polarization, with no transmitter.
interactions.yields: Surface and atmospheric temperature; emissivity, hence composition; vertical profiles when the emitting gas is also the absorber (sounding); energy deposition (aurora); activity (fires, lights, transmitters); plasma populations (energetic neutral atoms).
interactions.limit: One radiance measurement contains two unknowns, temperature and emissivity, so separation needs multiple bands, angles or a model (split-window, temperature–emissivity separation). Radiometric noise in the microwave scales as T_sys/√(B·t), which fixes dwell and bandwidth. Weak emissions are observable only at night in bands where sunlight competes.

interactions.name: Elastic scattering
interactions.note: Photons redirected by particles, density fluctuations or rough surfaces with no change of wavelength
interactions.physics: The regime is set by the size parameter x = 2πr/λ. Rayleigh (x ≪ 1): molecules, intensity ∝ λ⁻⁴, strongly polarized at 90°. Mie (x ~ 1): aerosol and cloud droplets at optical wavelengths, hydrometeors at microwave; the phase function and polarization encode size, shape and refractive index. Geometric and Bragg (x ≫ 1): radar backscatter from surfaces, where resonant Bragg scatter from capillary waves gives the wind signal in scatterometry.
interactions.observable: Scattered intensity as a function of angle, wavelength and polarization; range-resolved when the source is pulsed (lidar, radar).
interactions.yields: Particle size distribution, concentration and phase (aerosol, cloud, precipitation); surface roughness and dielectric constant (radar backscatter); wind over water; vertical structure of cloud and aerosol layers.
interactions.limit: The inverse problem from intensity alone is ill-posed; angle, polarization or multiple wavelengths are needed to separate size from concentration. Multiple scattering in dense media confounds single-scatter retrievals. Attenuation along the path couples the return at depth to everything above it.

interactions.name: Inelastic (fluorescence, Raman, Brillouin, nuclear)
interactions.note: Energy changes in the interaction: fluorescence, Raman, Brillouin, nuclear excitation
interactions.physics: Fluorescence: a photon is absorbed and re-emitted at longer wavelength after internal relaxation; chlorophyll fluoresces at 685 and 740 nm. Raman: a photon scatters with a wavelength shift equal to a vibrational or rotational quantum of the molecule, about 10⁻³ of the elastic cross-section. Brillouin: scattering from thermally excited acoustic waves, shifted by a few GHz in water, set by sound speed. Nuclear: galactic cosmic rays spall nuclei in regolith, which emit characteristic gamma lines and neutrons.
interactions.observable: Emission at a shifted, species-specific wavelength or energy, separable from the elastic return by a filter, etalon or spectrometer.
interactions.yields: Unambiguous species identification (Raman shifts, gamma lines); plant physiological state (solar-induced fluorescence); water temperature (Brillouin shift); elemental abundance and hydrogen content of regolith (gamma and neutron lines).
interactions.limit: Cross-sections are small, so the photon budget decides everything from orbit: Raman is roughly a thousand times weaker than Rayleigh and Brillouin weaker still. Fluorescence needs a pump bright enough to compete with reflected background, which is why solar-induced fluorescence is measured inside Fraunhofer lines where the background is dark.

interactions.name: Refraction & occultation
interactions.note: Ray bending by refractive-index gradients, read along a limb-grazing path
interactions.physics: Refractive index varies with density, water vapor and, at radio frequencies, electron density. A ray grazing the limb bends toward the denser medium; the bending angle as a function of impact parameter inverts (Abel transform) to the refractivity profile. The same geometry gives extinction versus tangent height, differential refraction, and scintillation from turbulence. Ionospheric dispersion delays lower frequencies more, which is how dual-frequency GNSS measures electron content.
interactions.observable: Carrier phase and Doppler of a coherent source behind the limb (GNSS-RO), bending angle, intensity versus tangent height (solar and stellar occultation), scintillation spectrum, differential group delay.
interactions.yields: Refractivity, hence density, pressure and temperature in the stratosphere and upper troposphere; humidity in the lower troposphere given a temperature prior; electron density profiles; turbulence strength; trace gases in occultation.
interactions.limit: Needs a source behind the limb and a receiver in front, so sampling depends on orbital geometry. Vertical resolution is excellent (~100 m) but the measurement averages ~200–300 km along the ray. Temperature and humidity are not separable in the lower troposphere from refractivity alone. Multipath and super-refraction at the boundary layer.

interactions.name: Doppler
interactions.note: Frequency shift from relative motion between source, scatterer and receiver
interactions.physics: A reflector moving at radial velocity v_r shifts a monostatic return by Δf = 2v_r/λ; the bistatic form is v·(k̂_s − k̂_i)/λ. Measurement needs a frequency reference narrower than the shift: a coherent local oscillator (heterodyne lidar, radar), a narrow spectral line (airglow, Fraunhofer lines on the Sun), or a received carrier (GNSS, RF emitters for frequency-difference-of-arrival).
interactions.observable: Shift, or spectrum of shifts, of a line or carrier of known rest frequency; for a pulsed system, the Doppler centroid and spectrum of each range gate.
interactions.yields: Wind profiles (lidar, airglow lines); ocean surface currents (along-track interferometry); hydrometeor fall speed and convective motion (Doppler radar); machinery vibration (vibrometry); inter-satellite range rate, hence gravity (GRACE); emitter location (FDOA); helioseismology on the Sun.
interactions.limit: Platform velocity of 7.5 km/s produces shifts far larger than most geophysical signals, so pointing knowledge and orbit knowledge set the floor. The reference must be narrower than the shift, which rules out sunlight reflected from Earth targets. Coherent integration time is bounded by speckle decorrelation.

interactions.name: Polarization
interactions.note: Orientation of the field vector, changed by reflection, scattering, emission, or magnetized media
interactions.physics: Reflection polarizes according to the Fresnel coefficients, strongly near Brewster's angle. Rayleigh scattering is fully polarized at 90°; Mie polarization depends on size and shape. Thermal emission from a smooth surface is partially polarized, the complement of its reflectance. In magnetized plasma, Faraday rotation turns the plane of polarization in proportion to electron content times the parallel field; in a magnetic field, spectral lines Zeeman-split into polarized components.
interactions.observable: The Stokes vector (I, Q, U, V) at optical and microwave wavelengths; the full scattering matrix (HH, HV, VH, VV) for polarimetric radar.
interactions.yields: Aerosol size, shape and refractive index; cloud thermodynamic phase; separation of surface roughness from dielectric constant (polarimetric decompositions); ocean wind direction (WindSat); oil and wet surfaces; magnetic field strength (Zeeman, Faraday); ionospheric electron content.
interactions.limit: The polarized fraction of most natural signals is a few percent, so instrument polarization and calibration accuracy dominate the error budget. Optical polarimetry needs three or more analyzer states or a modulator, each costing throughput or time. Faraday rotation is a nuisance for L-band radar unless it is the product.

interactions.name: Phase & coherence
interactions.note: Phase of a coherent field against a reference: interferometry, aperture synthesis, correlation
interactions.physics: A coherent field keeps a definite phase relative to a reference. Comparing phase between two apertures (cross-track interferometry, VLBI) or between two passes (repeat-pass InSAR) measures path-length differences to a fraction of a wavelength. Coherently summing returns along a trajectory synthesizes an aperture as long as the path (SAR); cross-correlating many small antennas synthesizes a filled aperture (SMOS). Second-order coherence (intensity correlation) recovers angular structure from photon-arrival statistics without phase-stable optics.
interactions.observable: Interferometric phase modulo 2π, coherence magnitude, fringe visibility, and the complex visibility across a baseline.
interactions.yields: Topography at meter scale (single-pass InSAR); surface deformation at millimeter scale (repeat-pass); three-dimensional structure in canopies and ice (tomography); terrestrial reference frame baselines to millimeters (VLBI); spatial resolution far beyond the physical aperture (SAR, aperture-synthesis radiometry); surface velocity (along-track interferometry).
interactions.limit: Both measurements must be mutually coherent: temporal decorrelation (vegetation, snow, water), atmospheric phase screens, and baseline knowledge all enter directly. Phase is ambiguous modulo 2π, so unwrapping is required. At optical wavelengths the platform must be known to λ/8 (~100 nm) over the synthesis time, which no orbital navigation achieves, so optical aperture synthesis from LEO is physics-dubious without a reference return.

interactions.name: Time of flight & delay
interactions.note: Propagation delay of a pulse or code from a known emission time
interactions.physics: Range follows from delay, R = cΔt/2 for a round trip. A one-way delay works when the clocks are synchronized (GNSS) or the source is periodic and modeled (pulsars). Differential delay between two frequencies isolates dispersive media (ionosphere); differential delay between receivers locates an emitter (time-difference-of-arrival). Photon-counting detectors extend the method to single-photon returns and time-tag each one.
interactions.observable: Round-trip or one-way delay of a pulse, chirp or code; the shape of the returned waveform over a sloped or rough footprint; the arrival-time histogram of single photons.
interactions.yields: Sea-surface height and ocean topography; ice-sheet and land elevation and their change; river and lake levels; precise orbits and the terrestrial reference frame (laser ranging); electron content (dual-frequency delay); emitter geolocation; canopy height and near-shore bathymetry (photon counting).
interactions.limit: Timing precision converts directly to range: 1 ns is 15 cm one-way. Propagation delays in the troposphere and ionosphere must be measured or modeled to the same level. Waveform shape over sloped, rough or vegetated footprints biases the retrieval. Passive time-difference methods need a shared time reference across receivers.

interactions.name: Penetration
interactions.note: Radiation entering below the first surface and returning information from depth
interactions.physics: Depth of penetration is set by attenuation. In water it is the diffuse attenuation coefficient, giving tens of meters in clear water for blue-green light. In soil, sand and vegetation the skin depth at radio wavelengths grows as √(λ/σ), so L- and P-band pass through canopy and dry ground where C- and X-band do not. HF and VHF penetrate kilometers of cold ice and dry regolith. Cosmic rays excite the top meter of regolith. Long-period electromagnetic induction reaches the crust and mantle.
interactions.observable: A depth-resolved return from a pulsed sounder, or an integrated signal whose weighting with depth is known (microwave radiometry, satellite-derived bathymetry, neutron albedo).
interactions.yields: Bathymetry; forest biomass and structure; soil moisture in the top centimeters; subsurface layering, paleochannels and buried ice; ice-sheet thickness and basal conditions; regolith composition; crustal and mantle conductivity.
interactions.limit: Longer wavelengths penetrate deeper but need larger antennas and give coarser resolution. Earth's ionosphere reflects below ~10 MHz, which is why radar sounding of Earth's subsurface from orbit is blocked while it works at Mars and the Moon. Conductive or turbid media stop everything at the surface. The surface signal must be separated from the subsurface one.

interactions.name: Field coupling (gravity, magnetic, relativistic)
interactions.note: A field, or a relativistic effect, sensed through its action on a proof mass, atom, clock, plasma, or orbit
interactions.physics: Gravity acts on a proof mass, on an atom in free fall, and on the orbit itself; its gradient is read by comparing two proof masses on a rigid baseline, its variation by ranging between two spacecraft. The magnetic field is read by a fluxgate or by the precession or level splitting of atoms and molecules (Zeeman effect, optically pumped magnetometers) and by Faraday rotation of a traversing wave. Electric fields and plasma are sampled directly. General relativity makes a clock's rate depend on the geopotential, 1.1×10⁻¹⁸ per centimeter of height.
interactions.observable: Acceleration, acceleration gradient, inter-satellite range rate, vector and scalar field magnitude, Zeeman line splitting, polarization rotation, clock frequency, particle cutoff rigidity.
interactions.yields: The geoid and its time variation (groundwater, ice mass, ocean bottom pressure); the core, crustal and ionospheric magnetic fields and the current systems driving them; electron content; geopotential height; radiation-belt and magnetospheric state.
interactions.limit: Field harmonics attenuate with altitude as (R/r)^(n+1), so spatial resolution is tied to orbit height and the lowest useful orbits fight drag. Non-gravitational accelerations must be measured or removed (drag-free control, accelerometers). Internal and external field sources must be separated. A potential field measured above its sources is smooth and non-unique at depth, so there is no image, only an inversion with priors.

techniques.name: Multispectral VNIR imaging
techniques.summary: Reflectance in a handful of bands; land cover, vegetation indices, water quality, change detection. The workhorse.

techniques.name: Hyperspectral VSWIR imaging
techniques.summary: Contiguous spectra resolve mineral, vegetation-biochemistry and plume absorption features; EMIT retrieves methane point sources from SWIR absorption.

techniques.name: SWIR trace-gas spectrometry (CO2, CH4)
techniques.band: 1.6 and 2.0 µm bands, 0.76 µm O2 A-band
techniques.summary: Column-average mixing ratio from line-by-line absorption depth against the O2 A-band as an airmass reference.

techniques.name: UV–Vis DOAS trace gases
techniques.summary: Differential optical absorption for NO2, SO2, O3, HCHO, BrO; geostationary versions now give hourly air-quality maps.

techniques.name: Solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence
techniques.band: Fraunhofer in-filling at 757/771 nm, FLEX at 687/760 nm
techniques.summary: Photosynthesis re-emits ~1% of absorbed light in the red/far-red; measured as filling-in of solar Fraunhofer lines. Direct proxy for gross primary productivity.
techniques.trlNote: OCO-2 and TROPOMI retrievals are operational; FLEX, the dedicated mission, is not yet launched.

techniques.name: Multi-angle reflectance / BRDF
techniques.summary: Same scene at several view angles constrains surface anisotropy, aerosol height (via parallax) and cloud-top height.

techniques.name: Multi-angle polarimetric aerosol/cloud retrieval
techniques.examples: POLDER/PARASOL, PACE HARP2 and SPEXone, 3MI, MAIA
techniques.summary: Degree and angle of linear polarization vs scattering angle pin down aerosol size, refractive index and shape far better than intensity alone.

techniques.name: Stereo photogrammetry
techniques.examples: SPOT HRS, ASTER, Pleiades, WorldView, Maxar Vivid 3D
techniques.summary: Along- or across-track image pairs give DEMs at sub-meter to 30 m posting; the optical route to topography.

techniques.name: Solar occultation spectroscopy
techniques.summary: Sun viewed through the limb at sunrise/sunset; self-calibrating (exo-atmospheric reference every event), very high vertical resolution, sparse sampling.

techniques.name: Limb scatter
techniques.summary: Sunlight scattered from the limb gives vertical profiles of ozone, aerosol and NO2 with daily global coverage that occultation cannot.

techniques.name: Sun-glint roughness and slick mapping
techniques.summary: Specular return maps ocean surface slope statistics; oil slicks and internal waves appear as glint contrast.

techniques.name: High-cadence video from orbit
techniques.summary: Tens of seconds of 30 fps imagery; vehicle tracking, plume dynamics, super-resolution from frame stacking.

techniques.name: Shortwave broadband radiation budget
techniques.summary: Absolute reflected-solar flux for climate energy balance; the calibration problem is the whole problem.

techniques.name: Ocean color
techniques.summary: Water-leaving radiance after atmospheric correction gives chlorophyll, CDOM, sediment; sunlight penetrates the first optical depth (a few to tens of meters).

techniques.name: Satellite-derived bathymetry
techniques.summary: Depth from the ratio of blue and green bottom-reflected radiance in clear water to ~20–30 m.

techniques.name: Solar Doppler and magnetograms
techniques.examples: SDO HMI, SOHO MDI, Hinode SOT
techniques.summary: Target is the Sun itself: Fraunhofer-line Doppler shifts give helioseismology; Zeeman polarization gives vector magnetic fields. Fills the Sun × Doppler and Sun × field cells only for the Sun as target.

techniques.name: Coronagraphy and heliospheric imaging
techniques.summary: Thomson-scattered photospheric light traces coronal mass ejections through the heliosphere; space-weather remote sensing.

techniques.name: Thermal infrared imaging
techniques.examples: Landsat TIRS, ASTER, ECOSTRESS, VIIRS, SLSTR
techniques.summary: Brightness temperature to surface temperature and emissivity; evapotranspiration, urban heat, volcanic and industrial thermal state.

techniques.name: Active-fire and hotspot detection
techniques.examples: MODIS, VIIRS, FireSat, SLSTR, GOES ABI
techniques.summary: Planck-curve contrast at 4 µm makes sub-pixel fires detectable; fire radiative power scales with emitted flux.

techniques.name: Thermal-IR hyperspectral sounding
techniques.summary: Thousands of channels across CO2 and H2O bands invert to temperature and humidity profiles; the single largest positive impact on NWP forecast skill.

techniques.name: Passive microwave imaging radiometry
techniques.summary: Conically scanned brightness temperatures through clouds: SST, sea ice, snow, precipitation, soil moisture. WindSat's third and fourth Stokes parameters retrieved wind direction.

techniques.name: Microwave temperature and humidity sounding
techniques.summary: Channels up the wings of the O2 and water lines weight different altitudes; all-weather profiles complementing IR sounders.

techniques.name: L-band radiometry (soil moisture, salinity)
techniques.summary: Dielectric contrast of water at 1.4 GHz; emission originates from the top ~5 cm of soil. SMOS synthesizes a 69-element Y-array by cross-correlation, the one flown correlation receiver for Earth emission.

techniques.name: Sub-mm and THz limb sounding
techniques.examples: Aura MLS, Odin SMR, SMILES, ISS
techniques.summary: Heterodyne limb radiometry resolves rotational lines of O3, ClO, HCl, H2O, CO in the stratosphere and mesosphere.

techniques.name: Zeeman-split O2 mesospheric sounding
techniques.summary: The geomagnetic field Zeeman-splits O2 lines; retrievals above ~40 km must model the field, and conversely the split encodes it.
techniques.trlNote: Flown and modeled in operational sounders, but as a correction; the field itself is not a delivered product.

techniques.name: Longwave and far-IR radiation budget
techniques.summary: Outgoing longwave; the far-IR beyond 15 µm carries half of it and was unmeasured spectrally until PREFIRE.
techniques.trlNote: Broadband longwave is TRL 9 (CERES). Spectrally resolved far-IR: the PREFIRE CubeSats launched 2024-05/06, L1–L3 products are public, spectral OLR was validated in peer review (JGR Atmospheres 2026), and the mission was extended through at least 2026-09; TRL 9 as of 2026-10. FORUM, the full-resolution far-IR FTS, is contracted for a late-2027 Vega-C launch.

techniques.name: Thermal inertia mapping
techniques.summary: Day–night temperature amplitude inverts to thermal inertia: rock vs soil, moisture, and shallow subsurface structure.

techniques.name: Airglow and aurora imaging
techniques.band: FUV 135.6 nm, O 557.7/630 nm, OH bands
techniques.examples: GOLD, ICON, TIMED GUVI, DE-1, Polar UVI
techniques.summary: Chemiluminescent layers at 85–300 km image gravity waves, tides, ionospheric bubbles and auroral energy input.

techniques.name: Airglow Doppler winds
techniques.examples: UARS WINDII, TIMED TIDI, ICON MIGHTI
techniques.summary: Doppler shift of airglow emission lines via Fabry–Pérot or Doppler asymmetric spatial heterodyne gives thermospheric winds at 90–300 km.

techniques.name: Energetic neutral atom imaging
techniques.summary: Charge exchange turns ring-current ions into neutrals that fly straight; imaging them maps the magnetosphere's plasma from a distance.

techniques.name: Nighttime lights
techniques.examples: DMSP OLS, VIIRS DNB, SDGSAT-1, Jilin-1 night
techniques.summary: Anthropogenic light as the signal: economic activity, electrification, conflict, fishing fleets, gas flares (with SWIR).

techniques.name: Passive RF geolocation and spectrum monitoring
techniques.summary: TDOA/FDOA across a cluster locates emitters (radars, AIS-dark vessels, jammers); the emission itself is the observable.

techniques.name: Optical lightning mapping
techniques.examples: TRMM LIS, GOES GLM, MTG LI, FY-4 LMI
techniques.summary: Continuous 500 fps imaging of lightning optical pulses from GEO; storm intensification precursor.

techniques.name: Lightning O2 A-band cloud-top height
techniques.summary: Lightning light exiting through the cloud is absorbed by O2 in the column above; the depth gives the emission altitude.
techniques.trlNote: Flight data exists (GLM, ISS-LIS, ASIM) but the height retrieval is research-grade, not an operational product.

techniques.name: Terrestrial gamma-ray flashes and TLEs
techniques.summary: Relativistic runaway electron avalanches in thunderstorms produce MeV photon flashes; sprites and elves imaged from the ISS.
techniques.trlNote: Inelastic added 2026-10-17: the TLE half of this entry (sprites, elves, halos imaged by ISUAL and ASIM) is lightning-pumped N2 emission, so the technique also fills the natural-transients × inelastic cell.

techniques.name: VLF sferics and whistlers for ionospheric sounding
techniques.examples: DEMETER, Van Allen Probes EMFISIS, C/NOFS
techniques.summary: Lightning-generated waves propagate through the ionosphere and along field lines; dispersion measures plasma density along the path.

techniques.name: Coseismic ionospheric disturbances
techniques.summary: Quakes, tsunamis, volcanic explosions and rocket launches launch acoustic-gravity waves that perturb TEC minutes later; detected via GNSS delay.
techniques.trlNote: Detected routinely after events in research; no operational warning product.

techniques.name: Synthetic aperture radar imaging
techniques.band: P, L, S, C, X, Ka
techniques.examples: Sentinel-1, RADARSAT, TerraSAR-X, ICEYE, Capella, Umbra, NISAR
techniques.summary: Coherent along-track aperture synthesis gives meter-class resolution day/night through cloud; backscatter encodes roughness, dielectric, geometry.

techniques.name: Repeat-pass and persistent-scatterer InSAR
techniques.summary: Interferometric phase between passes resolves mm/yr deformation: subsidence, volcanoes, earthquakes, infrastructure.

techniques.name: Single-pass cross-track InSAR DEM
techniques.summary: Two receivers separated across-track see the same pulse; phase difference maps topography with no temporal decorrelation.

techniques.name: Along-track interferometry
techniques.examples: TerraSAR-X ATI, SRTM ATI, Sentinel-1 experimental
techniques.summary: Two apertures separated along-track by milliseconds measure radial surface velocity: ocean currents, moving-target indication.
techniques.trlNote: Experimental modes on TerraSAR-X and Sentinel-1; no operational along-track product.

techniques.name: Polarimetric SAR
techniques.summary: Full scattering matrix decomposes into surface, double-bounce, volume; crop type, biomass, sea ice classification.

techniques.name: SAR Faraday-rotation TEC
techniques.summary: The ionosphere rotates polarization in proportion to TEC × B; a calibration nuisance for PolSAR that doubles as a TEC map.
techniques.trlNote: Demonstrated with PALSAR data as a calibration byproduct.

techniques.name: SAR tomography
techniques.summary: Many baselines resolve the vertical scattering profile inside forest canopies and ice; 3D SAR.
techniques.trlNote: TanDEM-X multi-baseline experiments gave the first spaceborne tomograms. Biomass has been acquiring 7-image tomographic stacks since 2025-11-21 (phase runs to 2027-04); tomographic L2B height and biomass products are scheduled for 2027-05 and no on-orbit tomograms were published as of 2026-10. TRL 8; re-check at the L2B release.

techniques.name: Low-frequency penetrating SAR
techniques.summary: Long wavelengths pass through canopy and dry sand or ice; forest biomass, subsurface paleochannels, ice-sheet structure.
techniques.trlNote: L-band is long-standing TRL 9 (ALOS-2/4, SAOCOM, NISAR). P-band from orbit: Biomass launched 2025-04-29, commissioning complete and L1 products open 2026-01, first L2A forest-height product 2026-06; TRL 9 as of 2026-10. Above-ground-biomass L2B product scheduled 2027-05.

techniques.name: Radar altimetry
techniques.summary: Pulse round-trip to sea surface at cm precision; sea level, ocean circulation, ice elevation. SAR-mode (delay-Doppler) sharpens along-track.

techniques.name: Wide-swath interferometric altimetry
techniques.summary: Two antennas on a 10 m boom interferometrically resolve height across a 120 km swath; rivers, lakes, sub-mesoscale ocean.

techniques.name: Scatterometry
techniques.summary: Backscatter vs azimuth from capillary waves gives ocean-surface wind vectors; also soil moisture and sea-ice type.

techniques.name: Cloud profiling radar
techniques.summary: Vertical profiles of cloud water and ice; EarthCARE adds Doppler for fall speeds and convective motion.

techniques.name: Precipitation radar
techniques.summary: Dual-frequency ratio separates drop size from rain rate; the reference for global precipitation.

techniques.name: Radar sounding of subsurface and ice
techniques.summary: HF/VHF pulses penetrate km of ice and dry regolith; not usable on Earth from orbit because the ionosphere blocks HF.
techniques.trlNote: Mission-proven at Mars and the Moon; not applicable to Earth from orbit.

techniques.name: Topside ionospheric sounder
techniques.summary: Swept-frequency HF reflects at the plasma frequency; electron-density profiles above the F2 peak.

techniques.name: Photon-counting lidar altimetry
techniques.summary: Single-photon time-tagging at 10 kHz: ice-sheet height change, canopy structure, and incidental bathymetry to ~40 m.

techniques.name: Atmospheric backscatter lidar
techniques.examples: CALIPSO CALIOP, EarthCARE ATLID (HSRL), ACDL (China, HSRL)
techniques.summary: Elastic backscatter profiles aerosol and cloud layers; high-spectral-resolution variants separate molecular from particulate return for absolute extinction.

techniques.name: Doppler wind lidar
techniques.summary: Line-of-sight wind from Doppler shift of molecular and aerosol backscatter; the first direct global wind profiles.
techniques.trlNote: Single mission (Aeolus, 2018–2023); laser degradation was a known issue; Aeolus-2 in development.

techniques.name: IPDA / DIAL greenhouse-gas lidar
techniques.summary: On/off-line pulse pairs give column CO2 or CH4 day, night and at high latitude where passive SWIR fails.
techniques.trlNote: CO2 IPDA: ACDL on DQ-1 (launched 2022-04-16) has produced global XCO2 since 2022, validated against TCCON at about 0.2 ppm bias and 1.5 ppm RMSE in 2025–26 literature; TRL 9 for CO2 as of 2026-10. CH4 IPDA at 1645 nm remains unflown; MERLIN launch is listed for 2028–2029.

techniques.name: Satellite and lunar laser ranging
techniques.summary: Ground stations range to retroreflectors at mm precision; defines the terrestrial reference frame origin and tests gravity.

techniques.name: Inter-satellite microwave and laser ranging
techniques.summary: Range-rate between two co-orbiting spacecraft at nm/s maps time-variable gravity: groundwater, ice mass, ocean bottom pressure.

techniques.name: Electrostatic gravity gradiometry
techniques.summary: Six accelerometers on a rigid frame measure second derivatives of the geopotential; static geoid to 1–2 cm at 100 km.

techniques.name: Gravity from precise orbit determination
techniques.examples: CHAMP, Swarm, LAGEOS, every geodetic satellite
techniques.summary: Orbit perturbations invert to the gravity field; the oldest space-geodetic observable (Vanguard's pear-shaped Earth, 1958).

techniques.name: Vector and scalar magnetometry
techniques.summary: Fluxgate plus absolute scalar (Overhauser or He-4) instruments map the core, crustal and ionospheric fields; Swarm's He-4 magnetometer is a flown quantum sensor.

techniques.name: Electric field and plasma instruments
techniques.examples: Swarm EFI, DMSP SSIES, C/NOFS, MMS
techniques.summary: Langmuir probes, ion drift meters and double probes sample the plasma the spacecraft flies through; in-situ but treated as remote sensing of the ionosphere.

techniques.name: Energetic particle detectors and cutoff rigidity
techniques.examples: GOES SEISS, Van Allen Probes, PAMELA, AMS-02
techniques.summary: Geomagnetic cutoff of cosmic-ray arrival directions maps the field's shielding; radiation-belt dynamics from particle spectra.

techniques.name: Planetary gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy
techniques.examples: Lunar Prospector, Mars Odyssey GRS/HEND, MESSENGER, LRO LEND, Dawn GRaND
techniques.summary: Galactic cosmic rays excite nuclei in the top meter of regolith; leaked gamma lines and neutron albedo give elemental abundance and hydrogen. Earth's atmosphere is too thick for this from orbit.

techniques.name: Cosmic-ray air-shower fluorescence from orbit
techniques.summary: Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays make N2 fluoresce along the shower; the same fast UV cameras see transient luminous events and meteors.
techniques.trlNote: Mini-EUSO (ISS, 2019–) and TUS operated in orbit and observed TLEs and meteors; after five years Mini-EUSO reports no confirmed UHECR detection (arXiv 2601.11458, 2026-01). No orbital successor is scheduled; the POEMMA balloon flies 2027. TRL 6 as of 2026-10.

techniques.name: Stellar occultation
techniques.examples: GOMOS (Envisat), UVS instruments at planets, New Horizons
techniques.summary: Star setting behind the limb gives ozone, NO2 and density profiles; hundreds of stars nightly, self-calibrating.

techniques.name: Geodetic VLBI
techniques.summary: Cross-correlating quasar signals at ground stations measures baselines to mm and Earth orientation; the only flown correlation receiver using a cosmic source. Space-VLBI (RadioAstron) extended the baseline.

techniques.name: Pulsar-timing navigation
techniques.summary: Millisecond pulsar arrival times fix spacecraft position to ~km; positioning rather than Earth sensing, but it fills the cosmic × time-of-flight cell.
techniques.trlNote: SEXTANT demonstrated on the ISS (2018).

techniques.name: GNSS radio occultation
techniques.examples: COSMIC-2, Metop GRAS, Spire, PlanetiQ, GeoOptics
techniques.summary: Bending angle of GNSS rays through the limb inverts to refractivity, then temperature and moisture at ~100 m vertical resolution, bias-free.

techniques.name: GNSS reflectometry
techniques.summary: Delay-Doppler maps of forward-scattered GNSS signals give ocean wind, soil moisture, flooding, sea ice; a bistatic radar with free transmitters.

techniques.name: Polarimetric GNSS-R
techniques.examples: Airborne campaigns, SMAP radar-receiver reuse studies
techniques.summary: Polarization ratio of the reflected signal separates dielectric from roughness effects for soil moisture and vegetation.
techniques.trlNote: Airborne campaigns only.

techniques.name: GNSS-R altimetry and snow/ice sensing
techniques.examples: TDS-1 altimetry, CYGNSS sea-ice, ground GNSS-IR snow depth
techniques.summary: Delay of the specular point gives dm-level surface height; L-band penetrates dry snow so the reflection encodes depth.
techniques.trlNote: TDS-1 altimetry demonstrated in orbit at research grade; ground GNSS-IR snow depth is operational.

techniques.name: Ionospheric TEC from dual-frequency GNSS
techniques.summary: Dispersive delay between frequencies is proportional to electron content along the path; the backbone of ionospheric monitoring.

techniques.name: Passive bistatic radar with broadcast illuminators
techniques.examples: Ground and airborne demos; passive SAR with Starlink downlinks in the literature
techniques.summary: Correlate a reference channel against surface echoes of a comm or broadcast signal to image or track with no transmitter of your own.
techniques.trlNote: Ground and airborne demonstrations only, including Starlink-illuminated passive SAR imagery (IEEE JSTARS 2024) and a German MoD Starlink passive radar (2024-01); no orbital receiver has flown and none is on a near-term manifest. TRL 5 as of 2026-10.

techniques.name: Free-space optical link scintillometry
techniques.summary: Intensity fluctuations on satellite–ground laser links measure integrated turbulence and extinction; characterized per link, not yet used as a sensing network.
techniques.trlNote: Characterized on OICETS, LCRD and EDRS links; not yet used as a sensing product.

techniques.name: Interferometric aperture-synthesis radiometry from GEO
techniques.summary: A sparse array correlated in real time synthesizes a filled aperture for microwave sounding from GEO, where a mechanical dish would be impractically large.
techniques.trlNote: GeoSTAR and GIMS/GIMS-II are ground demonstrators. China's FY-4M geostationary microwave sounder is planned for 2026–30 (CMA, 2026-04), and the published design descriptions found point to a 5 m real-aperture sounder rather than aperture synthesis, though that reading could not be confirmed from the primary paper. TRL 5 as of 2026-10; re-check at FY-4M launch.

techniques.name: Cold-atom accelerometry demonstration
techniques.summary: Atom-interferometer accelerometers have operated in microgravity; the step to a gradiometer is the concept in the next list.
techniques.trlNote: Atom-interferometer inertial sensing has been demonstrated in orbit: NASA CAL dual-species interferometry (ISS, Nature 2023) and CSSAI on Tiangong (cold-atom gyroscope and accelerometer, about 1 µm s⁻² and 17 µrad s⁻¹, 2024–25). Gravimetry-grade performance has not been shown; the CARIOQA pathfinder is in Phase B for an early-2030s launch. TRL 7 as of 2026-10.

techniques.name: Hosted star-tracker exploitation
techniques.examples: Space-domain awareness from commercial star trackers
techniques.summary: Sunlit debris and satellites streak through star-tracker fields; existing hardware repurposed for orbit determination.
techniques.trlNote: On-orbit star-tracker data exploited for SDA.

techniques.name: Raman lidar (ground and airborne)
techniques.examples: Ground Raman lidars, airborne water-vapor Raman
techniques.summary: Vibrational Raman return gives water vapor and temperature without assumptions; from orbit the photon budget is roughly 10³× short.
techniques.trlNote: Ground Raman lidar is TRL 9. From orbit the photon budget fails by ~10³; studies only.

techniques.name: Laser-induced fluorescence lidar (ocean, vegetation)
techniques.summary: Pulse-excited fluorescence of chlorophyll, CDOM and oil gives composition the elastic return cannot.
techniques.trlNote: Airborne oceanographic and oil-spill fluorosensors.

concepts.name: Rydberg-atom RF electrometry from orbit
concepts.physics: Atoms excited to Rydberg states have enormous electric dipole moments. An RF field resonant with a Rydberg transition splits the electromagnetically-induced-transparency line by the Rabi frequency, which is set by the field amplitude and a known dipole matrix element. The readout is therefore self-calibrated to SI units, tunable from ~MHz to THz, and needs no wavelength-sized antenna.
concepts.application: Broadband passive microwave radiometry and RF geolocation in a CubeSat volume; THz limb sounding without heterodyne front-ends.
concepts.failure: Sensitivity still trails cryogenic LNAs by an order of magnitude or more; laser and vapor-cell reliability in vacuum and radiation. The win is bandwidth and calibration, not noise floor.
concepts.first: Compare noise-equivalent field against a state-of-the-art radiometer at 6, 37 and 183 GHz for the same integration time.
concepts.prior: Spaceborne Rydberg-atom RF sensing is the target of funded agency programs: NASA NIAC Phase I/II Quantum Rydberg Radar (JPL, 2023; balloon demonstration planned), NASA ESTO's QuARREM Rydberg hyperspectral radiometer (Infleqtion, 2025), ESA's RYDAR receiver prototype (Warsaw, 2025), and ground soil-moisture reflectometry with satellite signals of opportunity (Arumugam et al., Sci. Rep. 2024). No on-orbit flight reported. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Lab and field demos of Rydberg receivers; no space-environment validation.

concepts.name: Orbital laser Doppler vibrometry
concepts.physics: A heterodyne lidar resolves surface velocity via Δf = 2v/λ; at 1.5 µm, 1 mm/s is 1.3 kHz. Machinery, engines and structures vibrate at characteristic frequencies that show up as sidebands on the return.
concepts.application: Industrial activity monitoring, centrifuge-hall and generator signatures, bridge and dam modal health.
concepts.failure: Platform velocity of 7.5 km/s and speckle decorrelation limit coherent integration to microseconds. Needs a co-located reference return (a static surface or retroreflector) for differential measurement, and dwell long enough to resolve the vibration lines.
concepts.first: Speckle decorrelation time vs spot size and orbital velocity, then the achievable frequency resolution per dwell.
concepts.prior: Proposed by JPL as an orbital vibrometer for ground targets (NASA Tech Briefs, 2009) and claimed as a space use in a Caltech/NASA patent (US 8,210,044, 2012); the orbital speckle-noise problem was analysed for asteroid seismology by Courville (Adv. Space Res., 2019). Airborne and vehicle LDV are demonstrated; no orbital demonstration against Earth targets found. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Airborne LDV validates the sensor, not the orbital speckle-decorrelation problem.

concepts.name: Space-to-sodium-layer magnetometry
concepts.physics: Sodium atoms at 85–95 km, excited by a 589 nm laser, precess in the geomagnetic field at the Larmor frequency. Modulating the laser at that frequency drives spin polarization and changes fluorescence; sweeping the modulation finds the resonance and hence |B| to nT.
concepts.application: Global mesospheric magnetometry along track; a layer no in-situ instrument occupies, sensitive to ionospheric current systems.
concepts.failure: Laser power and beam quality from orbit; fluorescence photon budget at 500+ km; competing OH and background light. Ground systems already do this with 20 W lasers over ~90 km paths.
concepts.first: Fluorescence photon rate at the spacecraft for a 20 W CW laser and a 1 m aperture; compare to shot-noise requirement for 1 nT.
concepts.prior: Ground sodium-layer magnetometry was proposed by Higbie et al. (PNAS 2011) and demonstrated by Kane et al. (JGR 2018). A satellite-assisted variant with the laser on the ground and a polarimeter in LEO was proposed by Dang et al. (2021). The all-from-orbit configuration with the laser on the spacecraft has not been proposed in detail or flown. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground LGS magnetometry proves the physics; space geometry untested.

concepts.name: Powerline flicker sensing from orbit
concepts.physics: LED and discharge lamps modulate at twice the mains frequency (100 or 120 Hz) with modulation depth of a few to tens of percent. A photon-counting array sampled above 300 Hz on a small nighttime field of view recovers the modulation frequency and phase.
concepts.application: Map which regions run on which synchronous grid; detect islanding, generator-powered sites, and frequency excursions that precede grid stress; identify off-grid installations.
concepts.failure: Photon rate is not the limit (see TRL basis). The risks are platform: holding a 100 m cell for a second from LEO needs body pointing or back-scan, pointing-jitter power near 100–120 Hz masquerades as signal, and mixed lamp types can dilute the modulation depth below 1 %.
concepts.first: Photon rate for a 100 m ground pixel at typical urban radiance with a 30 cm aperture; SNR at 120 Hz over a 1 s dwell.
concepts.prior: Flicker-based grid sensing is established from the ground (Bianco et al., NYC hypertemporal imaging, 2016; Sheinin et al., ICCP 2018). From orbit, Elvidge et al. (Remote Sensing 2022) showed that VIIRS DNB's millisecond dwell aliases lighting flicker into nightly radiance variance without resolving frequency or phase. No spaceborne or airborne sensor sampling above Nyquist to recover mains frequency was found; the earlier airborne claim did not survive a search. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: First calculation run 2026-10-17 (scripts/calc/c04_powerline_flicker.py). A 30 cm aperture at 500 km collects about 3×10⁶ detected photons per second from a 100 m urban pixel at 100 nW cm⁻² sr⁻¹ and 3×10⁵ from a suburban one. With 10 % effective modulation the 120 Hz line has SNR of order 100 and 40 over a 1 s stare, and depths below 1 % stay detectable. Photons are not the limit; TRL 3 on the analytic budget. Untested: the 1 s stare on a 100 m cell against 7 km s⁻¹ ground motion, and pointing jitter near 100–120 Hz.

concepts.name: Opportunistic laser occultation via constellation crosslinks
concepts.physics: A laser crosslink between two satellites at different orbital shells or planes can graze the limb. Refractive bending, scintillation spectrum and weak-line absorption at 1550 nm encode density, temperature, turbulence and (weakly) water vapor and CO2 along the tangent path.
concepts.application: Thousands of free occultation events per day from megaconstellations at optical wavelengths, complementing GNSS-RO with higher vertical resolution.
concepts.failure: Geometry: same-plane links at ~550 km have tangent heights near 500 km, above the atmosphere. Only inter-plane and inter-shell links graze low; link acquisition may drop the link before it reaches the troposphere. Comm lasers are fixed-wavelength, so absorption is limited to whatever lines fall in-band.
concepts.first: Sweep a real constellation's crosslink topology for tangent-height distribution vs time.
concepts.prior: Observed once, incidentally: the OICETS–ARTEMIS laser link of April 2006 recorded atmospheric power fluctuations as OICETS set behind the limb (Löscher, AMT 2010). Perlot and Sofieva (ICSOS 2009) proposed adapting laser-communication terminals for occultation sounding; Liu, Kirchengast et al. (2021) simulated LEO–LEO occultation statistics; the dedicated ACCURATE laser-occultation mission was proposed to ESA in 2005 and not selected. The megaconstellation tangent-height census has not been done. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Geometry study not yet done. The 2006 incidental occultation record on a comm link shows the signal exists in space; no retrieval has been attempted from it, so the TRL is left as judged.

concepts.name: Bistatic and multistatic lidar
concepts.physics: The aerosol and cloud scattering phase function varies strongly with angle and with particle size, shape and refractive index. A transmitter on one spacecraft and receivers on others sample off-axis angles that monostatic lidar cannot reach.
concepts.application: Direct microphysical retrievals of aerosol and cloud particles; ice-crystal habit; validation of the phase functions every radiative-transfer model assumes.
concepts.failure: Signal at off-axis angles is orders of magnitude weaker than backscatter; pointing and timing across free-flyers; multiple scattering contaminates at large angles.
concepts.first: Received photons per shot at 10°, 30° and 90° scattering angle for a representative aerosol layer and 1 m receiver.
concepts.prior: Concept papers only, as far as I know.

concepts.name: Chronometric geodesy with optical clocks
concepts.physics: General relativity: a clock's rate shifts by ΔU/c². One centimeter of height near Earth's surface is 1.1×10⁻¹⁸ in fractional frequency. Comparing an orbiting optical clock against ground clocks over optical links measures geopotential differences directly.
concepts.application: A geoid observable independent of mass-change ranging and gradiometry; unification of height systems across continents; tests of relativity.
concepts.failure: Requires 10⁻¹⁸ clock stability in orbit and a link that transfers time at the same level through the atmosphere; ACES (2025, ISS) works at 10⁻¹⁶ with microwave clocks.
concepts.first: Verify ACES results and link performance; cost the optical-clock and link upgrade.
concepts.prior: ACES launched to the ISS in April 2025 and, as of mid-2026, was still in commissioning with science data taken since October 2025 and no published clock-comparison result (ESA mission page; SYRTE announcement, May 2026). No optical clock has operated as a clock in orbit: the strontium lattice-clock optical system on the Chinese Space Station reached in-orbit laser stabilisation and a MOT (Rev. Sci. Instrum. 96, 2025); ESA's I-SOC Pathfinder is unscheduled. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground optical-clock chronometric geodesy demonstrated. ACES (ISS, 2025) is a microwave-clock pathfinder at the 10⁻¹⁶ level, still commissioning as of mid-2026. TRL 4 stands; re-check when the first ACES redshift or time-transfer paper appears, expected 2026–2027.

concepts.name: Single-spacecraft atom-interferometer gravity gradiometry
concepts.physics: Two cold-atom clouds separated by a baseline are interrogated with the same laser pulses; the differential phase gives the gravity gradient with no drift, since the reference is an atomic transition rather than a proof mass.
concepts.application: GOCE-class static gravity with long-term stability; sub-surface density mapping for aquifers, magma systems, voids.
concepts.failure: Sensitivity per shot is limited by atom number and interrogation time; rotation of the spacecraft couples in; the NASA and ESA pathfinders that would settle it are now 2030-class launches.
concepts.first: Check flight status of NASA QGGPf and ESA CARIOQA before doing anything else.
concepts.prior: Neither pathfinder has flown. NASA's QGGPf is contracted for a 2030 LEO launch (Infleqtion follow-on award, August 2026); ESA/CNES CARIOQA entered Phase B in October 2025 with an engineering-model laser source delivered September 2026 and launch in the early 2030s. The only orbital atom interferometer is CSSAI on the China Space Station (Li et al., National Science Review 2025), a single-sensor gyroscope and accelerometer at the µm s⁻² level, not a gradiometer. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground atom gradiometers exist and CSSAI (2025) validated cold-atom interferometry in orbit, which supports 5; no differential two-cloud gradiometer has been validated in a relevant environment, so 4 is defensible. Pathfinders slipped to 2030 and beyond, so the number will not move in this window.

concepts.name: Intensity interferometry of sunlit orbital objects
concepts.physics: Hanbury Brown–Twiss: intensity fluctuations at two apertures are correlated by |γ|², the squared degree of coherence, which encodes angular structure. Only nanosecond timing is needed, not optical phase stability, so baselines of kilometers between free-flyers are feasible.
concepts.application: Angular characterization of GEO objects from their solar glint; stellar astrometry. Earth-surface imaging is not viable because the source is not hot and bright enough.
concepts.failure: SNR scales with the square of the source brightness temperature and needs large photon rates; ground demos on stars took hours.
concepts.first: Photon rate from a glinting GEO satellite at a 1 m aperture and the integration time to reach |γ|² SNR of 5.
concepts.prior: Intensity-correlation imaging of sunlit GEO satellites has been studied since an AFRL-funded Texas A&M telescope reached first light on a star in 2008, with a pessimistic SNR analysis by Fried, Riker and Agrawal (JOSA A 2014) and design studies by Hyland (Appl. Opt. 2024); a free-flying space intensity interferometer for stars was analysed by Klein, Guelman and Lipson (2006). No satellite has been imaged this way. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground stellar intensity interferometry proves the physics.

concepts.name: Entanglement-assisted long-baseline optical imaging
concepts.physics: Gottesman–Jennewein–Croke (2012): a shared entangled photon pair lets two apertures interfere incoming light without physically transporting it between them, using a teleportation-style measurement. Removes the beam-transport loss that makes optical VLBI impossible.
concepts.application: Centimeter-scale resolution from GEO or beyond; the end-state for passive optical resolution limits.
concepts.failure: Entangled-pair rates must match the incoming photon rate per mode; quantum memories and repeaters at telescope scale do not exist; decades out.
concepts.first: Required entangled-pair rate for a given target photon flux and baseline.
concepts.prior: The scheme is Gottesman, Jennewein and Croke (PRL 2012); tabletop and 20 km fibre demonstrations on simulated thermal sources followed (Brown et al. 2023; Wang et al., USTC 2025), and a 2018 IAC conference paper (La Mura et al.) proposed entanglement-sharing space telescope arrays. No funded space study, mission or on-sky starlight demonstration found; the orbital application is an extrapolation of published work. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Theory and tabletop experiments.

concepts.name: Infrasound-in-airglow impulsive-event monitoring
concepts.physics: Explosions and large impulsive events launch infrasound and acoustic-gravity waves that reach 85–95 km within minutes and modulate OH and O airglow brightness by percent-level amounts.
concepts.application: A GEO airglow imager at high cadence becomes a passive global monitor for nuclear tests, volcanic explosions and large accidents, with arrival-time triangulation.
concepts.failure: Discriminating impulsive signatures from the dense background of gravity waves; nighttime only for most emissions; cloud contamination for nadir viewing.
concepts.first: Expected airglow modulation amplitude vs source yield and distance, against imager noise at 1 s cadence.
concepts.prior: Ground imagers and GOLD/ICON see gravity waves; a dedicated impulsive-event system has not flown as far as I know.
concepts.trlNote: Hunga Tonga (2022) acoustic-gravity waves were seen in airglow from ground and from GOLD/ICON.

concepts.name: Orbital magnetotelluric sounding of the crust
concepts.physics: Natural ionospheric current variations induce currents in the conductive Earth; the ratio of induced to inducing field vs period gives conductivity vs depth. Swarm has done this at mantle scale.
concepts.application: Regional crustal conductivity for geothermal and mineral targeting; basin-scale resistivity where no ground MT exists.
concepts.failure: Spatial resolution scales with altitude; crustal-scale needs a very low orbit (drag) or dense swarms; separating the induced field from ionospheric source structure.
concepts.first: Resolution vs altitude for a 3-satellite swarm at 250 km with 0.1 nT magnetometers.
concepts.prior: Mantle-scale induction from Swarm published; crustal-scale would be new.
concepts.trlNote: Mantle-scale induction from Swarm published.

concepts.name: Brillouin lidar for ocean temperature profiles
concepts.physics: Spontaneous Brillouin backscatter in water is shifted by ~7–8 GHz, proportional to sound speed, which is dominated by temperature. A narrow-linewidth green lidar with an edge-filter or heterodyne receiver returns a temperature profile through the top tens of meters.
concepts.application: Mixed-layer temperature structure, which satellites currently see only at the skin; ocean heat content and hurricane fuel.
concepts.failure: Brillouin cross-section is small and the water column attenuates; from orbit the photon budget is marginal at best. Likely lives on aircraft.
concepts.first: Photons per shot per 5 m depth bin from 500 km with a 1 m aperture and 1 J pulses.
concepts.prior: Laboratory profiling to 0.07 °C and 1 m was demonstrated by Rudolf and Walther (Opt. Eng. 2014). The US Navy funded an airborne Brillouin ocean-temperature lidar (BOLTS, SBIR N211-089, 2021–2025), NASA Langley published an airborne receiver concept (2024) and NASA Goddard ran observing-system simulations for ocean heat content (Remote Sensing 2024). No spaceborne instrument or satellite photon-budget study found; the airborne step this entry expected is already funded. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Lab and shipboard demos.

concepts.name: Umbra-station limb transmission spectroscopy
concepts.physics: Earth's umbra extends ~1.4 million km anti-sunward. A spectrometer inside it sees the Sun fully eclipsed with a refracted ring of limb-transmitted light: a continuous all-longitude transmission spectrum through roughly 100× the airmass of a nadir sounder.
concepts.application: Trace-gas limb profiles integrated around the whole terminator; Earth as an exoplanet analog for transit-spectroscopy validation.
concepts.failure: Station-keeping deep in the umbra; the ring is faint and refraction-limited below ~10 km tangent height; limited to terminator geometry by construction.
concepts.first: Ring radiance vs tangent height and the spectral resolution achievable with a 20 cm telescope.
concepts.prior: Mayorga et al. (PSJ 2021) proposed a small satellite beyond the Earth–Sun L2 point to observe Earth transiting the Sun in transmission at 0.2–2.5 µm; that vantage lies past the umbra tip, so it is a transit rather than this umbral refracted-ring geometry. Earth's limb transmission spectrum has otherwise been measured through lunar eclipses from the ground (Pallé et al. 2009) and from HST (Youngblood et al. 2020), and Kaguya imaged the refracted ring from lunar orbit in 2009. No spectrometer stationed inside the umbra has been proposed. Checked 2026-10-17.

concepts.name: Cosmic-ray radio pulses as impulsive illuminators
concepts.physics: Extensive air showers emit nanosecond broadband radio pulses (30–1000 MHz) via geomagnetic and Askaryan mechanisms. The ANITA balloon detected these reflected off the Antarctic ice sheet; the reflection's polarity and amplitude encode surface reflectivity and near-surface density.
concepts.application: Passive VHF/UHF ground-penetrating radar of ice sheets with nature's transmitter; potentially firn density and surface roughness.
concepts.failure: Event rate above threshold is low; the source position must be reconstructed per event; SNR at orbital altitude vs balloon altitude.
concepts.first: Rate of showers above 10¹⁸ eV per day within the footprint, and received field strength at 500 km.
concepts.prior: ANITA detected ice-reflected cosmic-ray radio pulses (Hoover et al., PRL 2010); Antarctic surface reflectivity was measured from the same payload with the Sun and a balloon pulser rather than cosmic rays (Besson et al. 2013, 2017); a JPL satellite concept (SWORD, 2013) studied orbital detection of the reflected pulses for cosmic-ray science; Shoemaker et al. (Ann. Glaciol. 2020) read anomalous ANITA events as subsurface firn reflections. No work uses the showers as a systematic illuminator for ice-sheet sensing. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: ANITA incidental detections serve as proof of concept.

concepts.name: Rotational Doppler via orbital-angular-momentum beams
concepts.physics: A beam carrying OAM ℓ reflected from a surface rotating at Ω acquires a frequency shift ℓΩ/π, independent of translational Doppler. Measures spin state directly.
concepts.application: Tumble rate of debris; reaction-wheel and rotor signatures of satellites; non-cooperative attitude determination.
concepts.failure: OAM beams need to overfill the target and preserve mode structure; divergence rules out ground targets from orbit; viable only at satellite-to-satellite ranges.
concepts.first: Mode purity after propagation to 100 km and the required target size for a given ℓ.
concepts.prior: Demonstrated in the laboratory by Lavery et al. (Science 2013) and extended to rough surfaces and about 1 km free-space range by Chinese groups (Opt. Express 2022 and later), with several papers treating non-cooperative rotating targets, tilt, offset and precession. No proposal or demonstration of satellite-to-satellite spin measurement of orbital objects found. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Laboratory demonstrations.

concepts.name: Ground laser guide star as calibrated overhead target
concepts.physics: A ground site excites a sodium-layer beacon at 90 km; a LEO imager views it from above. The result is a point source of known altitude, brightness and position, with the entire troposphere removed from the path.
concepts.application: MTF, geolocation and radiometric cross-calibration of commercial imagers; a second beacon gives a known baseline for stereo and pointing calibration.
concepts.failure: Beacon brightness from above is marginal for a 30 cm aperture at a 1 ms line time (SNR about 4) and comfortable from 50 cm up; radiometry needs a stare of order a second. The return is a single 589 nm line, so radiometric cross-calibration covers one band only. Scheduling against existing LGS sites; daylight operation impossible.
concepts.first: Beacon irradiance at 500 km for a 20 W laser and the resulting SNR for a 30 cm imager at 1 ms exposure.
concepts.prior: Psiaki, Flewelling and Hackett (NAVIGATION 2019) proposed that an orbiting camera observe a network of ground-pumped sodium guide stars as known-position references for autonomous orbit determination, the closest published use of a mesospheric beacon viewed from above. Ground lasers aimed directly at satellites have been used or patented for radiometric and polarisation calibration (NASA GSLC, 2014–2015) and geolocation alignment (GOES-R GLM beacons, 2015); Ball Aerospace patented a spacecraft-generated sodium guide star for telescope phasing (2001). No use of a ground LGS for MTF or radiometric calibration of a LEO imager found. Physics entirely off-the-shelf. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: First calculation run 2026-10-17 (scripts/calc/c17_laser_guide_star.py). A 20 W CW sodium laser returns about 10⁷ photons s⁻¹ m⁻² to a ground telescope, matching published returns, and 5×10⁵ photons s⁻¹ m⁻² at 410 km slant range. A 30 cm imager detects about 17 photons per 1 ms line, SNR 4, against negligible background through a 1 nm filter; 50 cm gives SNR 7 and 1 m gives 14. Centroiding and MTF work at the line rate with TDI; 1 % radiometry needs about 0.6 s of staring. TRL 3 on the analytic link budget; every component remains TRL 9.

concepts.name: Rayleigh–Brillouin lineshape lidar for temperature
concepts.physics: The spectral shape of molecular backscatter (Tenti S6 model) depends on temperature and pressure independently of any Doppler shift. A high-resolution Fabry–Pérot or etalon receiver on a UV lidar resolves the lineshape.
concepts.application: Temperature profiles with no radiosonde-style prior; a natural add-on to any Aeolus successor.
concepts.failure: Requires resolving ~GHz-scale features with adequate photon counts; aerosol Mie contamination in the boundary layer.
concepts.first: Photon-limited temperature precision per 1 km bin from an Aeolus-class transmitter.
concepts.prior: Ground demos; Aeolus used the Rayleigh channel for winds only.
concepts.trlNote: Ground Rayleigh–Brillouin lidar demos.

concepts.name: Ku/Ka reflectometry from megaconstellation downlinks
concepts.physics: GNSS-R at L-band senses ~20 cm roughness. Starlink and OneWeb downlinks at 12–20 GHz are ~10× stronger and ~10× shorter wavelength, sensitive to cm-scale roughness. The same illuminators enable passive bistatic SAR.
concepts.application: Wind stress, thin-film sea-ice state, snow wetness, soil moisture at finer scales; passive imaging with no transmitter.
concepts.failure: Beam-steered downlinks illuminate only user cells; waveform knowledge is proprietary, so a reference channel is required; ITU and provider consent.
concepts.first: Fraction of ocean surface illuminated at any instant by a real constellation's beam plan.
concepts.prior: Ground demonstrations exist: Starlink-illuminated passive SAR images from a fixed receiver (Gomez-del-Hoyo and Samczynski, IEEE JSTARS 2024) and Starlink/OneWeb signal characterisation for passive radar (Fraunhofer FHR, 2023–2024). Ku-band bistatic sea-state retrieval was shown earlier with GEO DirecTV signals (Shah et al., IEEE TGRS 2016). No geophysical retrieval from megaconstellation reflections, no airborne demonstration and no orbital receiver were found. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground passive-radar imaging with Starlink signals (2024) and Ku-band bistatic sea state from GEO signals (2016) validate the components; TRL 4. The earlier airborne-demo claim did not survive a search.

concepts.name: Lightning as a broadband in-atmosphere spectrometer source
concepts.physics: The lightning optical spectrum is known well enough that its appearance from space, after transit through cloud and the column above, encodes absorption. GLM already uses the O2 A-band for cloud-top height.
concepts.application: Water vapor and aerosol above cloud, at the place and instant of deep convection where soundings are weakest.
concepts.failure: Multiple scattering inside cloud smears the path length; spectral variability of lightning itself; low light for hyperspectral at 500 fps.
concepts.first: Information content of a 20-band lightning spectrum for water vapor above cloud top, with scattering path-length uncertainty included.
concepts.prior: Single-band flown; multiband not.

concepts.name: Laser-comm links as an aggregated turbulence and aerosol network
concepts.physics: Every satellite-to-ground laser link is a scintillometer: intensity variance and temporal spectrum give integrated Cn², and multi-aperture receivers give coarse profiles; mean loss gives aerosol extinction. Thousands of links are coming.
concepts.application: Global turbulence and aerosol climatology at no incremental cost; input to site selection and to optical-comm availability models.
concepts.failure: Adaptive optics and automatic gain control on operational links suppress the very signal being measured; data access from operators.
concepts.first: Which raw telemetry (pre-AGC power, tip-tilt residuals) an operator would need to expose.
concepts.prior: Characterized on individual links (OICETS, LCRD); nobody aggregates them as a sensing network, as far as I know.
concepts.trlNote: Individual-link characterization is the proof of concept.

concepts.name: Thermal-infrared Stokes polarimetry
concepts.physics: Emitted radiance from smooth surfaces is partially polarized by the Fresnel emissivity; degree and angle of linear polarization at LWIR give surface roughness and refractive index, and distinguish oil films, wet vs dry, and man-made vs natural.
concepts.application: Night, no-illumination material discrimination; oil-spill detection independent of sun glint.
concepts.failure: Instrument polarization and calibration at LWIR are hard; degree of polarization is only a few percent for most natural surfaces.
concepts.first: Expected degree of polarization vs view angle for water, oil and soil at 10 µm, against a realistic polarimetric accuracy.
concepts.prior: Airborne demos; I know of no orbital LWIR polarimeter, though I am less sure here than elsewhere.
concepts.trlNote: Airborne LWIR polarimeters.

concepts.name: Quantum illumination / quantum radar
concepts.physics: Entangled signal–idler pairs improve target detection in noise by up to 6 dB in error exponent at low signal-to-noise. The advantage requires retaining the idler and shrinks with loss.
concepts.application: Claimed: low-observable target detection.
concepts.failure: The advantage evaporates over kilometers of propagation loss and at microwave frequencies where thermal photons dominate; no path to orbital ranges.
concepts.first: None recommended; treat as killed unless a new mechanism appears.
concepts.prior: Laboratory demonstrations only: about 1 dB advantage at metre scale with cryogenic receivers (superconducting-circuit experiment, arXiv 2022). Independent analyses converge on a power-limited range ceiling: Shapiro's own review (arXiv 2019), Jonsson and Ankel (IEEE RadarConf 2021), and Pavan and Galati (Remote Sensing 2024), who put the intrinsic range for aircraft-class targets below 1 km and typically tens of metres. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Lab demos at metre scale. Physics-dubious at orbital ranges: the sub-photon-per-mode power ceiling caps range at well under 1 km in every published analysis, including the protocol originator's.

concepts.name: Synthetic-aperture lidar from LEO
concepts.physics: Aperture synthesis at 1 µm would give centimeter resolution from GEO in principle; it needs phase knowledge to λ/8 (~130 nm) across the synthetic aperture.
concepts.application: Claimed: SAR-class all-weather-independent resolution at optical wavelengths.
concepts.failure: Orbital motion compensation to 130 nm over the synthetic-aperture time is far beyond current navigation; atmospheric phase screens decorrelate in milliseconds. Airborne SAL worked over short paths.
concepts.first: Required motion-compensation accuracy vs available ephemeris and a reference-return scheme; if it cannot close by 10×, stop.
concepts.prior: Airborne SAL (Krause et al., CLEO 2011) remains the only flight demonstration; orbital SAL and ISAL exist only in simulation (Shen et al., Aerospace 2025). Published analyses limit the synthetic aperture to the atmospheric coherence length (JOSA A 2017; Sensors 2008). The most optimistic long-range study (Gao and Dong, Sensors 2024, about 3000 km with coherence compensation) concerns ISAL of space objects with no atmospheric path. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Airborne SAL (2011) validates optical aperture synthesis; orbital motion compensation unaddressed and the atmosphere caps the aperture at its coherence length. Physics-dubious for Earth-looking SAL from LEO.

sun|dopp.text: Sunlight reflected from Earth targets: 1 m/s is Δλ/λ ≈ 3×10⁻⁹, three orders of magnitude below Fraunhofer line widths. Filled only for the Sun as its own target (helioseismology).

sun|phase.text: Sunlight's spatial coherence area at Earth is tens of micrometers; target-side phase is unusable. Coherence across apertures (HBT correlation, C09) or quantum-projected interference (C10) is the only route.

sun|tof.text: No time reference in sunlight. Ruled out.

sun|emis.text: Emission from the target is by definition not the Sun as source; see Earth emission row.

earth|tof.text: Thermal emission carries no timing. Ruled out.

earth|phase.text: Thermal emission is incoherent at the target; phase is exploited only across apertures (aperture synthesis, T23 and T76), which the receiver axis captures.

earth|inel.text: Inelastic processes need a pump; Earth's thermal field pumps nothing observable. Ruled out.

earth|refr.text: Refraction bends limb-emission ray paths and is modeled as a correction. Whether refraction of emitted radiation carries independent information is unexplored.

earth|escat.text: Scattering of thermal photons by clouds and aerosol is part of every radiative-transfer model (e.g. cirrus retrievals) but not exploited as a standalone observable.

earth|abs.text: Filled via sounders: the absorbing gas is also the emitter.

own|emis.text: A transmitter does not make the target emit unless via laser-induced processes, which belong to the inelastic column.

own|refl.text: Radar and lidar returns are classified as elastic scattering here; specular reflection (calm water, retroreflectors) is a special case of the same column.

own|abs.text: Differential absorption lidar is the flown case; laser occultation (C05) extends it.

own|pen.text: Earth subsurface sounding from orbit is blocked by the ionosphere below ~10 MHz; the planetary sounders show what an ionosphere-free body permits.

soo|inel.text: Opportunistic sources lack the power density for fluorescence or Raman. Ruled out.

soo|fieldc.text: GNSS signals sense the ionosphere via refraction and Faraday rotation, not the field directly. A field-coupling observable from signals of opportunity is unexplored.

soo|refl.text: Reflectometry is classified under elastic scattering; the specular component is reflection in the narrow sense.

transient|escat.text: Lightning RF scattered from the ionosphere is observed incidentally (T36). No dedicated use.

transient|dopp.text: Doppler of lightning RF from ionospheric motion is measurable in principle; no technique recalled.

transient|pol.text: Lightning RF polarization after ionospheric transit encodes Faraday rotation; unexplored as a technique.

transient|phase.text: No phase reference for a natural impulsive source. Ruled out.

transient|tof.text: Multi-satellite TDOA on lightning sferics is done at ground level (WWLLN); a space-based version is unexplored.

transient|fieldc.text: Lightning-driven electron precipitation (LEP) couples to the magnetic field; observed in situ, not used as a remote technique.

cosmic|emis.text: Quasar and pulsar emission is the source; the cell is filled via VLBI and pulsar timing under phase and time of flight.

cosmic|dopp.text: No Doppler observable of an Earth target from a cosmic source. Ruled out.

cosmic|pol.text: Stellar or CMB polarization passing through the atmosphere is essentially unchanged; unexplored and probably empty for good reason.

cosmic|pen.text: Cosmic-ray muons penetrate rock but the detector must lie beneath the target (muography); from orbit only gamma and neutron leakage from the top meter is accessible, and only on airless bodies.

cosmic|refl.text: Air-shower radio pulses reflected off ice (C15) are the only candidate.

field|refl.text: Fields do not reflect. Ruled out.

field|refr.text: Gravitational lensing by Earth is ~10⁻⁹ rad; unusable. Ruled out.

field|pol.text: Zeeman polarization of emission lines (T16, T25) couples field and polarization; classified under those rows.

field|phase.text: Inter-satellite ranging (T58) and atom interferometry (C08) use phase as the readout of field coupling.

field|tof.text: Chronometric geodesy (C07) is time as the field observable: clock rate vs geopotential.

field|pen.text: Magnetotelluric induction (C12) is the penetrating case.

earth|refl.text: Downwelling atmospheric emission reflected by the surface is the (1−ε) term in every land-surface-temperature and microwave sea-surface retrieval: a correction that is modeled and removed, not an observable anyone retrieves. Whether the reflected component carries independent information (surface reflectance in the thermal IR, cloud-base emission mirrored by water) is unexplored from orbit.

transient|refl.text: Lightning and bolide light reaches orbit by multiple scattering through cloud (T33, T34), which the grid files under emission and absorption, not reflection. Specular reflection of a transient's light from water, ice or the sea surface would give an independent geometry on the source; no technique recalled uses it.

transient|inel.text: Filled via T35: sprites, elves and halos are nitrogen emission excited by the lightning electromagnetic pulse and quasi-static field, a secondary emission pumped by the transient, counted here as inelastic by the same logic that files sounders under both emission and absorption. TGFs themselves are bremsstrahlung and stay under emission.

filters.name: Photon budget
filters.text: The solid angle of a 1 m² aperture from 500 km is ~4×10⁻¹² sr. Any inelastic process (Raman, Brillouin, fluorescence) must clear roughly 10 detected photons per resolution cell after yield × aperture × dwell. Brillouin lidar (C13) is marginal; Raman from orbit is not viable.

filters.name: Coherence vs platform motion
filters.text: LEO moves 7.5 km/s. Coherent optical techniques need phase stability to λ/8 over the integration time, which limits coherent integration to microseconds without a reference return. Vibrometry (C02) and synthetic-aperture lidar (C24) live or die here.

filters.name: Diffraction and baseline
filters.text: Resolving centimeters from GEO at visible wavelengths needs ~100 m apertures or synthesized baselines. Intensity interferometry (C09) and entanglement-assisted imaging (C10) are the only routes and both are photon-starved.

filters.name: Illumination geometry
filters.text: Signals-of-opportunity concepts (C05, C15, C19) hinge entirely on where transmitters, tangent points and receivers align. An orbital-geometry sweep is the first analysis, before any link budget.

interactionNote: Classification conventions used throughout: reflection is the geometric-optics regime (reflector much larger than λ, surface-bound); elastic scattering covers particles, volumes and rough surfaces where the return depends on the size parameter, so radar and lidar backscatter sit there. Sounders that invert thermal emission through an absorbing gas are counted under both emission and absorption. Techniques that exploit phase only across apertures (aperture synthesis) are filed under emission with a correlation receiver, not under phase, which is reserved for cases where phase is itself the observable.
